items.parentTitle: Decimals Beyond Hundredths and Number Lines
items.whatStudentsLearn: In Level 5 Mathematics, children interpret, compare, and order decimals with more than two decimal places (thousandths), representing them accurately on number lines.
items.whatThisMeans: Understanding values smaller than hundredths. For example, knowing that 0.375 is between 0.37 and 0.38, and understanding that 0.5 is the same as 0.500.
items.whyItMatters: Essential for precision measurements in science experiments, swimming race split-times, and currency exchange.

homeActivities.title: Olympic Split Time Comparison
homeActivities.description: Look at swimming or sprint race results showing times to three decimal places (e.g. 21.345 s vs 21.350 s). Ask your child who was faster and by how many thousandths of a second.

items.whatStudentsLearn: Students express whole numbers as products of their factors, identify common multiples, and apply divisibility rules to determine if large numbers can divide evenly.
items.whatThisMeans: Finding all numbers that multiply to make a target (e.g. factors of 24 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24) and multiples (e.g. multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24...).
items.whyItMatters: Simplifying fractions, finding common denominators, and cryptography all rely on factors and prime numbers.

homeActivities.title: Factor Rainbow Game
homeActivities.description: Pick a number like 36 or 48. Draw an arc linking factor pairs from the outside in (1 × 36, 2 × 18, 3 × 12, 4 × 9, 6 × 6) to make a factor rainbow.

items.parentTitle: Multiplication and Division as Inverse Operations
items.whatStudentsLearn: Children recognise and explain the inverse relationship between multiplication and division, using it to build fact families and solve equations with unknown terms.
items.whatThisMeans: Knowing that if 7 × 8 = 56, then 56 ÷ 8 = 7 and 56 ÷ 7 = 8, enabling quick mental checks when dividing.
items.whyItMatters: Core foundational skill for high school algebra and rearranging formulas.

homeActivities.title: Multiplication Reversal Challenge
homeActivities.description: State a division problem like '72 divided by 9'. Ask your child what multiplication fact helps them solve it instantly (8 × 9 = 72).

items.parentTitle: Choosing Metric Units for Length, Mass, and Capacity
items.whatStudentsLearn: Students choose appropriate metric units when measuring length, mass, and capacity, converting between units (e.g. 1.75 kg = 1,750 g) to obtain accurate measurements.
items.whatThisMeans: Selecting the right tool and unit (e.g. metres for a room, millimetres for a screw, kilograms for body weight, millilitres for medicine).
items.whyItMatters: Daily life calculations in cooking recipes, home renovation, and medicine dosages.

homeActivities.title: Kitchen Unit Converter
homeActivities.description: Look at food packages in the kitchen (e.g. 500 mL cream, 1.5 L water, 750 g flour). Practice converting between litres and millilitres, or kilograms and grams.

items.parentTitle: Grid References, Coordinate Pairs, and Angle Types
items.whatStudentsLearn: Children locate positions using grid coordinates in the first quadrant, classify angles (acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex), and perform transformations (reflections, rotations, translations).
items.whatThisMeans: Using coordinate grids like (4, 7) and measuring turns in degrees (e.g. a right angle is 90°, a half turn is 180°).
items.whyItMatters: Foundational for computer programming, video game coordinates, digital mapping (GPS), and architecture.

homeActivities.title: Angle Spotter Walk
homeActivities.description: Look around your home or neighborhood. Spot acute angles (scissors opening slightly), right angles (corners of books), and obtuse angles (reclined chair).

items.parentTitle: Interpreting Data Displays, Mode, and Data Distributions
items.whatStudentsLearn: Students acquire, validate, and represent data using digital tools and spreadsheets, analyzing distributions in terms of highest frequency (mode) and shape.
items.whatThisMeans: Finding which value occurs most often in a dataset (the mode) and describing whether data is clustered in the middle or spread out.
items.whyItMatters: Crucial for science experiments, business sales analysis, and understanding statistical claims in news reports.

homeActivities.title: Family Shoe Size Mode
homeActivities.description: List the shoe sizes of everyone in your extended family or friend group. Identify the mode (the most common size).

items.subStrand: Equally Likely vs Non-Equally Likely Outcomes
items.parentTitle: Comparing Equally Likely and Unequally Likely Outcomes
items.whatStudentsLearn: In Level 5 Probability, students list all possible outcomes of chance experiments and distinguish between events that have an equal chance vs unequal chances.
items.whatThisMeans: Recognising that flipping a standard coin gives equally likely outcomes (50/50), whereas picking a colored marble from a jar with 9 blue and 1 yellow marble is unequally likely (90% vs 10%).
items.whyItMatters: Builds clear probabilistic thinking needed for game theory, financial risk, and science hypotheses.

homeActivities.title: Marble / Counter Bag Test
homeActivities.description: Put 8 red buttons and 2 green buttons in an opaque cup. Have your child explain why drawing a red button is much more likely than a green button.
